questions.stem: A Bendigo manufacturer's objective is to improve efficiency. Which human resource strategy most directly supports this objective?
options: training staff to use new equipment correctly so that less material is wasted
hiring more staff than are needed so that absences never slow down production
removing all performance targets so that staff feel less pressure at work
replacing all permanent staff with untrained casuals at short notice
questions.explanation: Well-trained employees use resources better, producing more output with less waste, which is what efficiency means. Hiring surplus staff raises labour costs for the same output, which works against efficiency.

questions.stem: Which lists the levels of Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs from lowest to highest?
options: physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualisation
safety, physiological, social, esteem, self-actualisation
physiological, safety, esteem, social, self-actualisation
physiological, social, safety, esteem, self-actualisation
questions.explanation: Maslow placed physiological needs at the base, then safety, social (belonging), esteem and finally self-actualisation at the top. A common slip is to swap social and esteem needs.

questions.stem: According to Maslow, which needs must be largely satisfied before social needs become a motivator?
options: esteem needs only
physiological and safety needs
esteem and self-actualisation needs
the drives to acquire and to defend
questions.explanation: Maslow argued that lower-level needs must be largely met before the next level motivates, so physiological and safety needs come before social needs. The drives to acquire and defend belong to Lawrence and Nohria's Four Drive Theory, not Maslow.

questions.stem: A manager promotes a high-performing employee to a new job title and announces the achievement at a staff meeting. Which level of Maslow's hierarchy is this most likely to satisfy?
options: physiological needs
esteem needs
safety needs
social needs
questions.explanation: Recognition, status and a respected title satisfy esteem needs, the fourth level. Social needs concern belonging and friendship, not status and recognition.

questions.stem: According to Maslow, why might a pay rise fail to motivate a well-paid employee who already has a secure job and good workmates?
options: her lower-level needs are already met, so only esteem and self-actualisation will motivate
money can motivate only after her self-actualisation needs have first been satisfied
pay meets the need for self-actualisation, and that need can never be satisfied at work
her drive to acquire is fully satisfied once she is paid more than the award rate
questions.explanation: Maslow held that a satisfied need no longer motivates, so once pay, security and belonging are met, only higher-level needs will drive her. Pay mainly meets lower-level needs, and the drive to acquire belongs to a different theory.

questions.stem: Which is one of the five principles of Locke and Latham's Goal Setting Theory?
options: the drive to defend
self-actualisation
performance-related pay
task complexity
questions.explanation: Locke and Latham's five principles are clarity, challenge, commitment, feedback and task complexity. The drive to defend is from the Four Drive Theory and self-actualisation is from Maslow.

questions.stem: A sales manager changes a team goal from 'sell more' to 'increase sales by 10 per cent by 30 June'. Which principle of Goal Setting Theory is she applying?
options: commitment
clarity
challenge
feedback
questions.explanation: Clarity means a goal is specific and measurable, with a clear timeframe, so employees know exactly what is expected. The goal is also more measurable, but the change from vague to specific is about clarity rather than difficulty.

questions.stem: A manager involves each employee in setting their own targets so that they accept the goals and want to achieve them. Which principle of Goal Setting Theory is this?
options: commitment
clarity
task complexity
feedback
questions.explanation: Commitment means employees understand and agree to a goal, which is more likely when they help to set it. Clarity concerns how specific the goal is, not whether employees accept it.

questions.stem: A Shepparton orchard manager meets pickers each week to show them how close they are to their targets and what they could improve. Which principle of Goal Setting Theory is applied?
options: feedback
challenge
commitment
clarity
questions.explanation: Feedback means giving employees regular information on their progress towards a goal so they can adjust their effort. Challenge concerns how difficult the goal is.

questions.stem: Staff at a Launceston bakery are set a daily target so easy that they reach it by midday. Which principle of Goal Setting Theory is not being met, and what is the likely effect?
options: clarity; the goal is too vague for staff to know when they have achieved it
task complexity; the task is too difficult for staff to achieve without training
feedback; staff have no way of knowing whether they have met the daily goal
challenge; an easy goal gives little sense of achievement, so motivation falls
questions.explanation: Goals should be difficult enough to stretch employees, and a goal reached by midday gives no challenge, so effort and motivation drop. Staff clearly know they have met it, so clarity and feedback are not the problem.

questions.stem: Engineers agree to a clearly worded goal to design a highly complex new system in two weeks, with weekly progress reports, but receive no extra time or training. Which principle suggests the goal is poorly set?
options: feedback
task complexity
clarity
commitment
questions.explanation: Task complexity means that complex goals need enough time and training so employees are not overwhelmed. The goal is clear, the engineers have agreed to it and they get weekly feedback, so only task complexity is breached.

questions.stem: Which lists the four drives in Lawrence and Nohria's Four Drive Theory?
options: physiological, safety, social and esteem
clarity, challenge, commitment and feedback
unfreeze, change, refreeze and review
acquire, bond, learn and defend
questions.explanation: Lawrence and Nohria proposed that people are motivated by the drives to acquire, to bond, to learn (comprehend) and to defend. Physiological, safety, social and esteem are levels of Maslow's hierarchy.

questions.stem: According to the Four Drive Theory, the drive to bond is best satisfied through:
options: fair and transparent processes for handling grievances
a culture of teamwork, friendship and belonging
a reward system that links pay closely to performance
jobs designed to be meaningful, varied and challenging
questions.explanation: The drive to bond is the need to form relationships and feel part of a group, so a supportive, team-based culture meets it. A reward system targets the drive to acquire, and fair grievance processes target the drive to defend.

questions.stem: A Sunshine Coast software firm redesigns jobs so that staff regularly tackle new problems and learn new skills. Which drive does this target?
options: the drive to bond
the drive to defend
the drive to learn
the drive to acquire
questions.explanation: The drive to learn is the need to satisfy curiosity and understand the world, so challenging, varied jobs that build skills meet it. The drive to acquire relates to obtaining rewards and status.

questions.stem: A business makes its performance reviews, promotion decisions and grievance procedures fair and transparent. Which drive does this mainly satisfy?
options: the drive to acquire
the drive to bond
the drive to defend
the drive to learn
questions.explanation: The drive to defend is the need to protect oneself and what one values, so fair, open processes make employees feel secure and justly treated. The drive to acquire is met by rewards such as pay and status.

questions.stem: According to Lawrence and Nohria, the drive to acquire:
options: is relative, so employees compare their rewards and status with those of others
is fully satisfied once an employee's basic physiological needs have been met
applies only to money and physical goods, and never to status or recognition
must be satisfied first, before the drive to bond can begin to motivate anyone
questions.explanation: The drive to acquire covers rewards and status, and it is relative, since people judge what they have against others. The drives are independent rather than ranked, so none must be satisfied before another can motivate.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the Four Drive Theory with Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs?
options: both theories hold that goals must be specific and challenging to motivate employees
both theories hold that financial rewards are the only real motivator of employees
the four drives are independent, while Maslow's needs are met in a set order
the four drives must be met in a set order, while Maslow's needs are independent
questions.explanation: Maslow argued that needs are met in a hierarchy from lowest to highest, while Lawrence and Nohria saw the four drives as independent and all active at once. Specific, challenging goals come from Locke and Latham.

questions.stem: Which is an example of performance-related pay?
options: coaching from a senior colleague to develop an employee's skills
a formal written warning issued to an employee for poor performance
promotion to a role with more responsibility and a new title
a bonus paid to staff who exceed their quarterly sales target
questions.explanation: Performance-related pay links financial rewards, such as bonuses, commissions and profit sharing, to results. Promotion is career advancement and a written warning is a sanction strategy.

questions.stem: A business sets out a clear path for staff to move into supervisor and management roles as they gain skills. Which motivation strategy is this?
options: a support strategy
a sanction strategy
performance-related pay
career advancement
questions.explanation: Career advancement gives employees the chance of promotion to higher positions, which tends to motivate in the long term. Support strategies, such as counselling and mentoring, help employees cope rather than offering promotion.

questions.stem: Offering confidential counselling, mentoring and flexible hours for staff with caring responsibilities is an example of:
options: support strategies
sanction strategies
performance-related pay
career advancement
questions.explanation: Support strategies help employees manage work and personal pressures, through counselling, mentoring and flexible arrangements. They do not involve financial rewards linked to output, which is performance-related pay.

questions.stem: Sanction strategies, such as warnings and the threat of demotion, usually motivate only in the short term because:
options: staff act out of fear, and resentment can lower morale over time
they are far too expensive for most businesses to use for long periods
they satisfy employees' self-actualisation needs for only a short time
a union must approve each sanction before management can use it
questions.explanation: Sanctions may bring a quick change in behaviour because employees fear the consequences, but they breed resentment and can damage morale and loyalty. They are cheap rather than expensive and do not meet any higher-level needs.

questions.stem: A Brighton real estate agency pays its agents a commission on every sale. Which is a likely disadvantage of this strategy?
options: every agent receives the same income regardless of how many homes they sell
it mainly satisfies the agents' self-actualisation needs rather than their pay
agents may compete with each other rather than cooperate
agents have no financial incentive to increase their personal sales results
questions.explanation: Commission rewards individual sales, which can lead agents to compete for clients and weaken teamwork. It gives a strong incentive to sell more and makes income depend on results, so the other statements are the reverse of how commission works.

questions.stem: Investment in training is often a long-term motivation strategy. Which is a disadvantage of it for the business?
options: it reduces employees' level of skill in the short term
staff may take their new skills to a competitor
it lowers employees' sense of being valued by the business over time
it can be used only for new employees and not for existing staff
questions.explanation: Training costs money and time, and once employees are more skilled they may be attracted to better offers elsewhere. Training usually makes employees feel valued and can be given to staff at any stage of their career.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of off-the-job training compared with on-the-job training?
options: experts can teach specialised skills and new ideas from outside the business
it costs less because no external trainer or course fee needs to be paid
the employee keeps producing output for the business while learning
the training is always tailored to the business's own equipment
questions.explanation: Off-the-job training gives access to specialist trainers and ideas the business may not have internally. It usually costs more and takes the employee away from production, and it may not be specific to the business's equipment.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of on-the-job training?
options: the employee must spend several days away from the workplace
course fees charged by external providers are usually high
the skills learnt may not suit the business's own equipment
the experienced worker may pass on bad habits to the trainee
questions.explanation: Because the trainee learns from a colleague, any poor practices that colleague has can be copied. Time away from the workplace and external course fees are disadvantages of off-the-job training.

questions.stem: A Melbourne accounting firm needs two staff to gain an advanced tax qualification that no one in the firm is able to teach. Which training option is most appropriate, and why?
options: on-the-job training, because it avoids any loss of working time for the staff
off-the-job training, because it is cheaper than training in the workplace
off-the-job training, because outside experts can teach knowledge the firm lacks
on-the-job training, because a colleague can demonstrate the skill as they work
questions.explanation: No one in the firm has the expertise, so on-the-job training is not possible, and an external course is needed. Off-the-job training is generally more expensive, so cost is not the reason to choose it.

questions.stem: Management by objectives involves:
options: a manager watching an employee perform their tasks to judge how well they work
an employee rating their own performance against a set of agreed criteria
issuing warnings to employees who fail to meet the targets set by management
a manager and an employee agreeing on goals and then reviewing progress against them
questions.explanation: Management by objectives has the manager and employee jointly set goals that align with business objectives, then monitor and review progress. Watching an employee work is employee observation, and self-rating is self-evaluation.

questions.stem: Before her annual review, a nurse completes a form rating her own performance against her goals for the year. This performance management strategy is:
options: management by objectives
on-the-job training
self-evaluation
employee observation
questions.explanation: Self-evaluation has the employee assess their own performance, often as preparation for a review. Employee observation involves a manager watching the employee at work, not the employee's own judgement.

questions.stem: A café manager watches a new barista over several busy shifts to judge his speed, accuracy and customer service. This performance management strategy is:
options: off-the-job training
employee observation
self-evaluation
management by objectives
questions.explanation: Employee observation involves a manager watching an employee perform their job to assess performance. Self-evaluation would have the barista judge his own work.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of appraisals as a performance management strategy?
options: they give employees no feedback at all on how they are performing in their role
they cannot be used to inform any decisions about pay or promotion
they require employees to set all of their own goals without managers
they take time and can be affected by the appraiser's bias
questions.explanation: Formal appraisals take management time to prepare and conduct, and the results depend on the judgement of the appraiser, which may be biased. Appraisals do give feedback and are often used for pay and promotion decisions.

questions.stem: Performance management can help achieve both business and employee objectives because it:
options: lifts productivity while identifying employees' training and reward needs
removes the need for managers to communicate with employees about their goals
guarantees that every employee will be promoted within a set period of time
lets the business set wages below the award for under-performing staff
questions.explanation: By setting and reviewing goals, performance management improves output for the business and shows where employees need training or deserve rewards. Wages below the relevant award are not lawful, whatever an employee's performance.

questions.stem: Redundancy occurs when:
options: an employee is dismissed for serious misconduct
an employee permanently leaves the workforce at the end of their career
an employee's job is no longer needed by the business
an employee chooses to leave to take up another job
questions.explanation: Redundancy is employer-initiated and happens when a position is no longer required, for example after a restructure or the introduction of technology. Choosing to leave is resignation, and leaving the workforce at the end of a career is retirement.

questions.stem: A warehouse worker in Dandenong is caught stealing stock and the employer ends his employment immediately. This type of termination is:
options: dismissal
redundancy
resignation
retirement
questions.explanation: Dismissal is initiated by the employer because of the employee's conduct or performance, and serious misconduct such as theft can justify ending employment without notice. Redundancy occurs when the job itself is no longer needed.

questions.stem: Which entitlement is paid when an employee is made redundant but not when an employee resigns?
options: redundancy (severance) pay
pay for accrued, unused annual leave
wages owed for hours already worked
superannuation owed on wages already earned
questions.explanation: Redundancy pay compensates an employee whose job has been abolished, so it does not apply to someone who chooses to leave. Accrued annual leave and wages owed are paid out whatever the reason for termination.

questions.stem: A business is making 30 staff redundant. Which is a transition consideration rather than an entitlement consideration?
options: offering outplacement services such as career counselling and help with résumés
paying out each employee's accrued, unused annual leave
calculating the period of notice owed to each employee
paying each employee the redundancy pay owed for their years of service
questions.explanation: Transition considerations help employees move on to the next stage, such as outplacement services, counselling and references. Leave payouts, notice and redundancy pay are entitlements the employee is owed.

questions.stem: Which statement about resignation is correct?
options: it can occur only once the employee has reached retirement age
it is the employee's own decision to leave, usually with notice given
it is initiated by the employer when the employee's job is no longer needed
it entitles the employee to redundancy pay for each year of service
questions.explanation: Resignation is the employee's own decision to leave, and the employee is normally expected to give the notice required by their award or agreement. A job that is no longer needed leads to redundancy, which is employer-initiated.

questions.stem: After 30 years with a Ballarat engineering firm, an employee plans to retire. Which is a transition consideration the employer could offer?
options: a redundancy payment calculated on each of her 30 years of service
a payout of her accrued, unused long service and annual leave
a final payment of the wages owed for the hours she has worked
a gradual reduction in hours and access to retirement planning advice
questions.explanation: Transition considerations ease the move out of the workforce, for example phased hours and retirement planning. Leave and wages owed are entitlements rather than transition support, and redundancy pay does not apply because the employee is choosing to leave.

questions.stem: Which is a role of the Fair Work Commission?
options: representing the interests of employees when they negotiate with employers
representing the interests of employers in national wage cases and disputes
running the payroll for businesses so that employees are paid the correct wages
approving enterprise agreements and helping to resolve workplace disputes
questions.explanation: The Fair Work Commission is Australia's national workplace relations tribunal: it approves enterprise agreements, makes and reviews awards and helps resolve disputes. Representing employees is the role of unions, and representing employers is the role of employer associations.

questions.stem: A group of Victorian hardware retailers joins a body that advises them on employment law and represents them at the Fair Work Commission. This body is:
options: a human resource manager
an employer association
a trade union
an enterprise agreement
questions.explanation: Employer associations represent and advise employers, including in matters before the Fair Work Commission. A trade union represents employees, not employers.

questions.stem: Which is a role of a human resource manager in workplace relations?
options: making legally binding decisions in disputes between other businesses
representing employees in their disputes against the business
negotiating agreements with employees and making sure the business meets its award obligations
setting the minimum wages and conditions that apply across a whole industry or occupation
questions.explanation: The HR manager acts for the business, negotiating with employees or their representatives and ensuring it complies with awards, agreements and the law. Setting industry minimums through awards is a role of the Fair Work Commission.

questions.stem: An award is:
options: a contract between two businesses for the supply of inputs
a legal document setting minimum pay and conditions for an industry or occupation
an agreement negotiated between one employer and its own employees at a workplace
an informal promise by a manager about future pay rises
questions.explanation: Awards, made and reviewed by the Fair Work Commission, set minimum pay and conditions for employees in a particular industry or occupation. An agreement negotiated at a single workplace is an enterprise agreement.

questions.stem: Before the Fair Work Commission approves an enterprise agreement, it must be satisfied that the employees covered are:
options: better off overall than under the relevant award
paid exactly the award rate with no other changes
all members of a registered trade union
employed on fixed-term rather than ongoing contracts
questions.explanation: The better off overall test checks that an enterprise agreement leaves employees better off overall than the relevant award. Union membership is not required, and an agreement can differ from the award as long as it passes the test.

questions.stem: A Geelong manufacturer and its employees negotiate higher pay in return for more flexible shifts, and the Fair Work Commission approves it. Compared with relying only on the award, this arrangement:
options: allows the business to pay below award minimums in exchange for more flexible shifts
removes any need for the Fair Work Commission to approve the terms of employment
applies the same pay and conditions to every business in the manufacturing industry
tailors wages and conditions to the business, while leaving staff better off overall
questions.explanation: An enterprise agreement lets an employer and its employees set conditions that suit their workplace, provided employees are better off overall than under the award. Conditions that apply across a whole industry describe an award.

questions.stem: In mediation, the independent third party:
options: represents the employees in their negotiations with the employer
decides which party must pay the legal costs of the other party
helps the parties reach their own agreement but does not impose a decision
hears both sides and then makes a decision that is legally binding on both
questions.explanation: A mediator helps the parties communicate and work towards their own solution, but has no power to impose an outcome. Hearing both sides and making a binding decision is arbitration.

questions.stem: Which sequence best reflects how a workplace dispute usually moves through the dispute resolution process?
options: arbitration first, followed by negotiation, and then mediation only as a last resort
direct negotiation, then mediation, then arbitration if agreement is still not reached
arbitration, then mediation, then direct negotiation if the decision is not accepted
mediation, then arbitration, then direct negotiation between the parties themselves
questions.explanation: Parties first try to settle the matter themselves, then use a mediator, and arbitration is the last resort because it takes the decision out of their hands. A binding arbitrated decision ends the dispute, so it would not come first.
